newsitem.title: USA: Search winds down for Texas tornado victims.
newsitem.headline: Search winds down for Texas tornado victims.

text.p: Rescuers on Thursday were wrapping up a search for victims of a devastating tornado that killed 28 people as it swept through Jarrell, Texas, two days ago, a police spokeswoman said.

Searchers combing the rubble of a subdivision in the central Texas town have found 27 bodies and remains believed to be that of another victim of the deadly twister, Texas Department of Public Safety spokeswoman Laureen Chernow said.
"We believe 28 people are dead," Chernow said. "There are additional remains they believe will turn out to be that of the 28th person."
Residents of the Double Creek Estates subdivision who survived the storm will be allowed to return to their shattered neighbourhood after police end the search for additional victims, Chernow said.
"(Rescuers) want to make one last swing (through the area) to make sure everything has been taken care of," she said.
Grief gripped this small Texas town on Thursday after officials began notifying families that their missing relatives were among the people killed by the storm.

"I know what I went through and I know what they went through. I just hope it happened fast for them," said Virginia Davidson, who survived the storm by huddling in a bathtub and covering herself with a blanket.

As the twister swept through the neighbourhood with winds of more than 200 mph (320 km), Davidson and the tub she was in were tossed 100 feet (30 metres) from her demolished house, but she survived with bruises and cuts, she said.
"I don't want to start over but we've got to," she said as she and her neighbours prepared to tour the devastation left behind in the town of 600 people 40 miles (64 km) north of Austin.

Other residents were growing restless to return to their homes, many of which were swept away as a line of storms spwaned at least six tornadoes that also killed two people and collapsed the roof of a grocery store near Austin.

Police have kept up a tight perimeter around the Jarrell neighbourhood, which is dotted with cement foundations where homes once stood, as they have searched since Tuesday for victims in a 4-mile- (6.4 km) long swath left by the storm.

"I've had it up to here with all this official crap. I can't get to my property, I can't run my business. It's just a mess and I've had just about all I can take," said Al Clawson, who owns a recycling business damaged in the storm.

James Taylor, a 38-year-old electrician, said he got a black eye when he was beaten with a police flashlight and arrested on Tuesday while trying to get to his home. "I was going to go back to see about my neighbourhood, to see about my property, to see about my house," he said. "They started whupping me."

Four victims have been positively identified and families of the dead on Wednesday night were led one by one into the white-frame First Baptist Church of Jarrell where local officials informed them of their loss.

Police, hindered by the difficulty in identifying the mangled bodies of the tornado victims, said the dead positively identified so far included a 5-year-old boy, a 44-year-old woman and two school-age brothers.

The delay had fostered hope among many here that their missing relatives had somehow survived when the tornado swept down a small valley on the outskirts of Jarrell and destroyed 50 homes. Adding to the uncertainty was a list of 23 people that police said were unaccounted for but not confirmed dead.

Max Johnson, pastor of the First Baptist Church, said the town's grieving process could now finally begin. "It has been kind of frustrating because of all the unknowns ... it's like a thorn in your foot you need to pull out," he said.

He said the dead were thought to include a family of five, all members of his church choir, who were trapped in their home when the giant tornado struck. "It's a terrible thing, but I believe that no matter what happens there's some good that come out of it," he said.
In this case, Johnson said, the good was subtle: "It kind of reminds us of how temporary we are."
